title: Coordinated Restoration Playbook and Customer Status Response Templates
author: Eleanor Park
body:
Purpose

This playbook standardizes multi-team restoration for incidents that affect customer-facing services. It focuses on coordinated detection, containment, restoration (stabilization), and customer communications. It is intended for SREs, on-call engineers, product incident leads, and customer success.

Scope

- Applies to incidents that meet Severity 2 (partial customer impact) and Severity 1 (widespread or critical outage) definitions.
- Includes guidance for multi-region failovers, degraded model-serving quality, and major latency regressions that affect SLAs.

Severity and Impact Matrix

Severity definitions (quick reference):

1) Severity 1 (S1) — Critical outage
- Symptoms: >80% customers affected, total service unavailability, data loss
- Initial SLO: Notify execs in 15 minutes; engage full incident command

2) Severity 2 (S2) — Partial degradation
- Symptoms: Significant latency increases for core endpoints, regional failures, intermittent 5xx spikes
- Initial SLO: Page primary on-call; incident lead within 30 minutes

3) Severity 3 (S3) — Minor / internal
- Symptoms: Single-customer issue, alert without customer impact
- Initial SLO: Triage in next business day or during on-call window

Roles & Responsibilities

- Primary On-call (Pager): First responder for alerts. Responsible for initial triage and immediate mitigation (5–15 minute goal for acknowledgement).
- Incident Lead (IL): Coordinates restoration and runbook execution; responsible for decision-making about rollbacks, mitigations, and customer comms cadence.
- Communications Lead (Comms): Owns status page updates and external customer messages. Coordinates with Customer Success for high-touch customers.
- Escalation Eng (SE): Specialist (serving/runtime/security) called for deep technical remediation.
- Postmortem Author (PA): Owns the RCA and action tracking within 5 business days after incident resolution.

Escalation Matrix (text table)

Condition | Primary | Escalation (5–30m) | Exec Alert (15–60m)
--- | --- | --- | ---
S1 site-wide outage | SRE on-call | Senior SRE / Runtime lead | CTO, Head of Product
S2 degraded latency | Service owner on-call | Performance team | Head of Platform (if >2 regions)
Suspected security incident | Security on-call | CISO on-call | Legal + Execs immediately

Quick Runbook: Detection → Stabilize → Restore

1) Detection & Triage (0–15m)
- Acknowledge and document alert in incident channel (#inc-<service>-YYYYMMDD).
- Primary On-call captures: initial symptoms, scope (regions/customers), current traffic patterns, and any recent deploys.
- If automated mitigations are available (circuit breakers, scaled-down routing), engage them immediately.

2) Containment (15–45m)
- Reduce blast radius: route around faulty region, disable risky feature flags, or switch to a previously validated model variant.
- Apply traffic shaping or rate limits for heavy endpoints.
- Gather telemetry: p95/p99 latency, error budgets, logs (20 mins snapshot), tracing spans for affected flows.

3) Stabilization and Restoration (45–180m)
- Incident Lead selects a restoration path: rollback, targeted restart, model swap, or capacity increase.
- Prioritize safety: prefer fallbacks that preserve data consistency.
- If using canary rollback, perform progressive traffic shifts (10%→30%→60%→100%) with 10 minute observation windows.
- Validate with synthetic traffic and golden prompt sets for model-quality regressions before re-opening full traffic.

4) Recovery and Monitoring (post-restore)
- Keep heightened monitoring for 24–72 hours (based on impact) with daily IL check-ins.
- Collect artifacts for postmortem: timeline, key logs, screenshots, metric graphs, and decision rationale.

Postmortem and RCA Guidance

- Timeline: Produce draft postmortem within 3 business days; final postmortem (with actions and owners) within 10 business days.
- Required sections: summary, impact (quantified customers, duration, SLA exposure, cost), timeline, root cause analysis, contributing factors, action items (owner and due date), detection and mitigation gaps, follow-ups.
- Severity change: If the postmortem changes the initial severity, annotate the reason and the approval from IL and Head of SRE.

Postmortem Template (text block)

---
Title: [Service] Incident YYYY-MM-DD
Author: [Name]
Severity: [S1|S2|S3]
Summary: Short description (1–2 sentences)
Impact: Number of customers, features impacted, regions, SLA exposures
Timeline: Timestamped events (UTC)
Root Cause: Concise technical description
Contributing Factors: List (3–6 items)
Action Items: - Action / Owner / Due Date
Detection & Response: Time to detect, time to mitigate, time to restore
Lessons Learned: Short bullets
---

On-call Rotation & Handover Best Practices

- Shift length: 7–10 days for primary on-call, 2–4 week for follow-on specialists depending on team norms.
- Handover checklist (every shift): ongoing incidents, flaky alerts, current experiments, temporary mitigations in place, and calendar conflicts.
- Escalation readiness: maintain contact details and backup on-call for critical services.
- Reduce fatigue: rotate high-intensity services on a quarterly schedule and measure mean time on-call (MTOC) to adjust staffing.

Game Day Program (quarterly)

Objective: Validate cross-team coordination for multi-component failures and refine runbooks.

Game day outline (single-day exercise):
- Pre-game brief (30m): scope, safety constraints, objectives
- Inject phase (60–90m): simulate realistic failure (e.g., region network partition, model-serving node crash, cache corruption)
- Operational response (90–120m): runbook execution, status updates, and customer comms
- After-action review (60m): collect notes, identify action items, assign owners
- Deliverable: updated runbook and one prioritized action with owner and due date

Metrics for success: time-to-detect, time-to-ack, time-to-restore, quality regression detection (for model issues), and accuracy of customer messages.

Status Page and Customer Communication Templates

Status page guidelines:
- Update cadence: every 15–30 minutes for S1; every 60 minutes for S2 until stabilization.
- Keep language plain and action-oriented; avoid speculative root causes.
- Include: impact summary, affected regions/endpoints, mitigation steps in progress, ETA (if available), and next update time.

Status Page Template (short)

Title: [Service] — Degraded performance affecting [feature/endpoints]
Impact: Partial service disruption impacting [X]% of customers in [regions] (e.g., increased latency, intermittent errors).
Current status: Engineers are actively investigating. We have applied [mitigation] to reduce customer impact.
Next update: in 30 minutes or earlier if there is progress.

Customer Email / CSM Templates

1) Initial high-touch customer alert (used by Customer Success + Comms Lead)
Subject: Incident: [Service] degradation — initial notice
Body:
Hi [Customer Name],

We are currently investigating degraded performance impacting [feature]. Our engineers are actively working on containment and restoration. At this time, you may see increased latency or occasional errors. We will provide the next update by [ETA]. If you see specific errors for your account, please reply and include request IDs or timestamps.

We apologize for the disruption and appreciate your patience.

Sincerely,
[Redwood Customer Success]

2) Status update (progress)
Subject: Update: [Service] restoration in progress
Body:
Hi [Customer Name],

A quick update: we have applied [mitigation], and metrics show [reduction in error rate / improved latency]. We are continuing validation and expect to restore full service in approximately [ETA]. We will follow up when service is fully restored.

If you require an incident call, let us know and we will arrange one.

Regards,
[Comms Lead]

3) Resolution and follow-up
Subject: Resolved: [Service] incident on [date] — next steps
Body:
Hi [Customer Name],

The incident affecting [service] has been resolved at [time UTC]. Impact: [X] customers affected, [Y] minutes of degraded service. We are preparing a post-incident report; the draft will be available by [date]. If you would like a tailored RCA for your usage, please request it and we will coordinate.

Apologies again for the disruption.

Best,
[Redwood Support / CS]

Runbook Ownership, Documentation, and Review Cadence

- Owners: each runbook must declare an owner (team and individual) and a secondary reviewer.
- Review cadence: runbooks for production-critical services (SLO-impacting) must be reviewed every 6 months and after any incident.
- Deprecation: any temporary mitigation or emergency toggle must have an automatic expiry (TTL) recorded and reviewed during handover.

Automation and Tooling Recommendations

- Incident channel templates and ephemeral doc generator: pre-create channels with a timestamped incident doc (linking to urgent dashboards).
- Synthetic canary checks that run golden prompt sets for model regressions and trigger automated paging if quality drops below threshold.
- Pre-approved playbooks for automated rollback and model variant swaps for the common failure modes.

Appendix: Useful Commands and Dashboards

- Create incident channel: /incident create --service <service> --sev <S1|S2> --lead <alias>
- Snapshot logs (example):
  aws logs start-query --log-group-name /aws/service --start-time <ts> --end-time <ts> --query-string "fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/"
- Canary validation script (example):
  curl -X POST https://api.internal.redwood/services/<service>/validate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"prompt": "hello"}'
